# Critic {#sec-critic}

[Learning from surprise]{.lb-subtitle}

<div data-life="status" data-stage="2.3"></div>

::: {.lb-takeaway}
**New:** cells that predict how good or bad the next moments will be, and a teaching signal that is the *surprise*:
what happened minus what was predicted. This is the role of dopamine.

**Result:** in a world whose poisons change, creatures with the critic eat more and live longer than creatures
taught by pain alone (10% more fitness, in all three seeds), and silencing the prediction of good things costs them
a fifth of it. In the lab the signal moves from the pain to its warning, as in recordings of dopamine cells.
:::

So far pain has been the teacher. Every painful bite strengthens the aversion to what the creature was looking at,
and nothing weakens it again. That works as long as the world keeps its promises. In this stage it does not: halfway
through a life the poison bushes turn good and the good ones turn poison. **A teacher that only speaks when it hurts
cannot say "this is no longer bad"**, so a creature taught by pain keeps avoiding what is now its best food.

The new teacher is a **critic**. It keeps an expectation and teaches with the difference. An expected pain teaches
nothing new; a pain that fails to come is a pleasant surprise, and that undoes the aversion.

<div data-life="brain" data-stage="2.3"></div>

## The circuit

- **Value cells** read the pallium and learn, within the life, how good (`value_app`) and how bad (`value_av`) the
  next few moments will be when a bush looks like this.
- **The surprise** is computed every tick: *taste − pain + prediction now − prediction a moment ago*. When things
  go as predicted the terms cancel. A bite that tastes better than predicted makes it positive; a pain, or a
  prediction that falls, makes it negative.
- **It teaches** the value cells, so the predictions improve, and every synapse that pain taught before (look and
  pallium onto the *bad* cells): a bad surprise strengthens the aversion, a good one weakens it.

In the model the surprise is a formula; in the brain it is the firing of dopamine cells. Building it from cells is
the next step.

## Biology

Dopamine cells in the midbrain fire a burst when something turns out better than expected and pause when it turns
out worse. In the classic recordings in monkeys they fire at a drop of juice; once a light reliably announces the
juice, they fire at the light instead; and when the juice is then left out, they pause at the moment it should have
come. This is the teaching signal of *temporal-difference learning*, a method from machine learning that predicted
these recordings.

Insects run the same scheme in the mushroom body (the counterpart of the pallium), with separate dopamine cells for
reward and for punishment. Mammals mostly signal both with one population of cells, as this model does.

## The world

The world of the pallium stage, with one change: at tick 800 of every life the two poison kinds of new bush turn
good and the two good kinds turn poison. Their looks stay the same.

<div data-life="settings" data-stage="2.3"></div>

## Did it work?

<div data-life="verdict" data-stage="2.3" data-used="value_app,value_av,no_plasticity"></div>

The critic pays: about 130 more fitness than the pain teacher when each lives alone, and about 180 more when the
two share a world. Its learning is needed (without any learning a fifth is lost), and so are the cells that
predict good things (`value_app`). The cells that predict bad things (`value_av`) are not used: pain arrives with
the bite, so there is little to predict about it ahead of time.

<div data-life="lines" data-stage="2.3" data-example="reversal_life"></div>

**Both kinds of creature switch.** After tick 800 both stop eating the bushes that turned poison and start eating
the ones that turned good, at almost the same rate. The pain teacher manages this in another way: a look that has
been seen often stirs the senses less, so an old aversion weakens on its own. The critic's creatures eat more
throughout, before and after the switch, and more of them are still alive at the end.

### In the lab

The theory makes sharp predictions, and they can be tested on one creature at a time. A new bush is put in front of
it; it bites three times and feels pain each time; after a pause the next trial begins.

<div data-life="lines" data-stage="2.3" data-example="dopamine_shift"></div>

**The surprise moves to the warning.** At the first painful meal the signal drops at the bites. After a few meals it
drops as soon as the bush appears, and much less at the bites. When the pain is then left out, the signal turns
positive where the pain should have been, as in the monkey recordings.

<div data-life="bars" data-stage="2.3" data-example="conditioning_lab" data-col0="critic" data-col1="pain teacher"></div>

**Extinction** (first two rows): when the pain stops, the critic's aversion fades by a third over twelve meals,
and the pain teacher's does not change. **Blocking** (last two rows) did not show: the theory predicts that a
second warning sign, added to one that already predicts the pain, is learned less. Here neither creature learned
the second sign at all in three bites, so there was nothing to block.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="All lesions"}
<div data-life="lesions" data-stage="2.3"></div>

The large losses for `value_app_prev` and `value_av_prev` are not a sign of use. These cells hold a copy of the
prediction a moment ago, and the surprise is the difference between the two. Silencing only the copy leaves an
error that never cancels, and this error unteaches every aversion.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The lab and the switch in numbers"}
<div data-life="table" data-stage="2.3" data-example="conditioning_lab"></div>
<div data-life="table" data-stage="2.3" data-example="reversal_bites"></div>
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What it took"}
- **A world that changes.** Where poison stays poison, the critic did no better than pain: pain comes at the bite,
  and a pain teacher learns from it directly. Unlearning is what only the critic can do.
- **The right moment.** The surprise of a tick is about the step that led to it, so it changes the synapses that
  were active a tick earlier (real synapses are changed by dopamine that arrives a second or two late).
- **A short horizon.** Nothing tells the creature how long a pain will last while the bush is in view, so the
  predictions look only a few ticks ahead. A sense of time since a warning is for a later stage.
- **Taste counts less than pain.** Whether a bite follows a look depends on a decision the pallium does not see, so
  taste can be only half predicted; at full weight the unpredicted taste drowned the lessons.
- **Wiring of its own.** The pallium's random wiring now belongs to the creature's place in the population, not to
  its genes, so no lineage can inherit a lucky code.
:::
